questions.text: DNA copying is essential during reproduction because:

options.text: It ensures transfer of characters and generates variations
It provides energy for cell division
It produces proteins for the organism

key_points: DNA copying transfers genetic information to the next generation
Variations generated during copying are basis for evolution
rubric.expected_answer: (b) It ensures transfer of characters and generates variations.

questions.text: Why is variation beneficial to the species but not necessarily for the individual?

key_points: Variations allow some individuals in a population to survive changing environments
A particular variation may not benefit a specific individual but helps the species survive as a whole
Example: heat-resistant bacteria surviving if water temperature rises
rubric.expected_answer: Variations are beneficial to the species because they enable some individuals to survive in changed environmental conditions, thus ensuring species survival. However, for an individual organism, a variation may or may not be useful — for example, heat-resistant bacteria survive warming water, but the variation is useless if temperatures remain normal.

questions.text: If the somatic (body) cells of an organism contain 48 chromosomes, how many chromosomes will be present in each gamete (reproductive cell) produced after meiosis?

key_points: Meiosis reduces chromosome number to half
Gametes are haploid cells
rubric.expected_answer: Number of chromosomes in each gamete = 48 / 2 = 24 chromosomes. During meiosis, the chromosome number is halved so that when two gametes fuse during fertilisation, the original diploid number is restored.

questions.text: Asexual reproduction takes place through budding in:

key_points: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Yeast

questions.text: Multiple fission is the mode of asexual reproduction observed in:

key_points: Plasmodium (malarial parasite) divides into many daughter cells simultaneously by multiple fission
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Plasmodium

questions.text: How does binary fission differ from multiple fission?

key_points: In binary fission, the parent cell splits into two equal daughter cells (e.g., Amoeba)
In multiple fission, the parent cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously (e.g., Plasmodium)
rubric.expected_answer: In binary fission, the parent organism splits into two daughter cells (e.g., Amoeba, Leishmania). In multiple fission, the parent cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously (e.g., Plasmodium). Binary fission produces two offspring while multiple fission produces many offspring at once.

questions.text: How will an organism be benefited if it reproduces through spores?

key_points: Spores are covered by thick walls that protect them until favourable conditions
Spores are light and can be carried by wind/water for dispersal
A single organism can produce many spores, increasing chances of survival
rubric.expected_answer: Spores are protected by thick walls that allow them to survive unfavourable conditions. They are light and produced in large numbers, which aids wide dispersal by wind and water. When conditions become favourable (moist surface), they germinate and grow into new individuals.

questions.text: Differentiate between binary fission in Amoeba and Leishmania. How does Plasmodium reproduce asexually?

key_points: In Amoeba, binary fission can occur in any plane as it has no fixed body shape
In Leishmania, binary fission occurs in a definite orientation (longitudinal) due to the whip-like flagellum
Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission — divides into many daughter cells simultaneously
rubric.expected_answer: In Amoeba, binary fission can take place in any plane since the organism has no fixed shape. In Leishmania, binary fission occurs in a definite orientation (along the longitudinal axis) because of its whip-like structure (flagellum) at one end. Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission, where the parent cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously.

questions.text: Can you think of reasons why more complex organisms cannot give rise to new individuals through regeneration?

key_points: Complex organisms have highly specialised and organised tissues/organs
They cannot simply divide cell-by-cell — specific cell types must be arranged in definite positions
Regeneration requires specialised cells that can dedifferentiate, which complex organisms lack in sufficient numbers
rubric.expected_answer: Complex multi-cellular organisms have specialised cells organised into tissues and organs placed at definite positions. They cannot regenerate from cut pieces because their body design requires specific organisation that cannot be recreated by simple cell division. Unlike Hydra or Planaria, they lack enough specialised regenerative cells to rebuild the entire body plan.

questions.text: Explain fission as a mode of reproduction in organisms. Describe with examples how binary fission occurs differently in Amoeba and Leishmania, and how multiple fission occurs in Plasmodium.

key_points: Fission is division of parent cell into daughter cells
Binary fission: parent splits into two equal daughter cells
Amoeba: fission in any plane (no fixed body shape)
Leishmania: fission in definite longitudinal orientation due to flagellum
Multiple fission: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells simultaneously
Cyst formation may occur in unfavourable conditions before multiple fission
rubric.expected_answer: Fission is a mode of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms where the parent cell divides into daughter cells. In binary fission, the cell splits into two equal halves. In Amoeba, this can occur in any plane since it has no fixed body shape. In Leishmania, which has a whip-like flagellum at one end, binary fission occurs in a definite longitudinal orientation. In multiple fission, as seen in Plasmodium (malarial parasite), the parent cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously. Under unfavourable conditions, Plasmodium forms a cyst and upon return of favourable conditions, undergoes multiple fission to produce many daughter cells at once.

partial_marks.3: All three organisms but lacking detail

questions.text: Draw a neat labelled diagram showing budding in Hydra. Briefly explain the process.

key_points: A bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site
The bud develops into a tiny individual
When fully mature, it detaches from the parent body and becomes an independent individual
rubric.expected_answer: In Hydra, budding occurs when a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at a specific site on the body. The bud gradually grows, develops tentacles, and forms a tiny individual. When fully mature, it detaches from the parent body and becomes a new independent organism.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Regeneration is not the same as reproduction.
Reason (R): Most organisms do not normally depend on being cut up to be able to reproduce.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: Regeneration and reproduction are different processes
Regeneration occurs when an organism is cut, but organisms don't rely on being cut to reproduce
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Regeneration is the ability to regrow from body parts when cut, but it is not a normal reproductive strategy. Organisms reproduce through other dedicated mechanisms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of vegetative propagation?

key_points: Bryophyllum reproduces vegetatively through buds on leaf margins
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Leaf buds in Bryophyllum. Buds produced in the notches along the leaf margin of Bryophyllum fall on the soil and develop into new plants — this is vegetative propagation.

questions.text: Why is vegetative propagation practised for growing some types of plants?

key_points: Plants raised by vegetative propagation bear flowers and fruits earlier than those from seeds
It enables propagation of plants that have lost the capacity to produce seeds (banana, orange, rose)
All plants produced are genetically similar to the parent plant, preserving desirable characteristics
rubric.expected_answer: Vegetative propagation is practised because: (1) Plants bear flowers and fruits earlier than those grown from seeds. (2) It allows propagation of plants that have lost the capacity to produce seeds, such as banana, orange, and jasmine. (3) All plants produced are genetically identical to the parent, ensuring desirable characteristics are maintained.

questions.text: The anther contains:

key_points: The anther is part of the stamen and produces pollen grains
rubric.expected_answer: (d) Pollen grains. The anther is the top part of the stamen and produces yellowish pollen grains containing male germ-cells.

questions.text: After fertilisation in a flower, the ovary develops into:

key_points: After fertilisation, the ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a fruit
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Fruit. After fertilisation, the ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a fruit, while the ovule develops into a seed.

questions.text: How is the process of pollination different from fertilisation?

key_points: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma of a flower
Fertilisation is the fusion of male germ-cell (from pollen) with female gamete (egg) in the ovule
Pollination precedes fertilisation
rubric.expected_answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. It can be self-pollination (same flower) or cross-pollination (different flower). Fertilisation is the fusion of the male germ-cell (from pollen grain) with the female gamete (egg cell) present in the ovule. Pollination is a prerequisite for fertilisation.

questions.text: What changes occur in a flower after fertilisation? Explain the formation of seed and fruit.

key_points: Zygote divides several times to form an embryo within the ovule
Ovule develops a tough coat and is converted into a seed
Ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a fruit
Petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off
rubric.expected_answer: After fertilisation: (1) The zygote divides repeatedly to form an embryo within the ovule. (2) The ovule develops a tough coat and gradually converts into a seed containing the embryo. (3) The ovary grows rapidly and ripens to form a fruit. (4) The petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma usually shrivel and fall off.

questions.text: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination. Name two agents of pollination.

key_points: Self-pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma of the same flower
Cross-pollination: transfer of pollen from one flower to another flower
Agents: wind, water, animals/insects
rubric.expected_answer: Self-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower. Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower. Two agents of pollination are wind and insects.

questions.text: Describe the process of sexual reproduction in flowering plants, starting from the structure of a flower to the formation of a seed. Include the roles of pollination, pollen tube growth, and fertilisation.

key_points: Flower has stamen (male) with anther producing pollen, and pistil (female) with stigma, style, and ovary
Ovary contains ovules with egg cells
Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma (self or cross)
Pollen grain germinates on stigma, pollen tube grows through style to reach ovary
Male germ-cell fuses with female gamete in ovule — fertilisation
Zygote divides to form embryo; ovule becomes seed; ovary becomes fruit
rubric.expected_answer: A flower contains stamens (male) and pistil (female) as reproductive parts. The anther of the stamen produces pollen grains. The pistil consists of stigma, style, and ovary. The ovary contains ovules, each with an egg cell. During pollination, pollen is transferred from anther to stigma by wind, water, or animals. The pollen grain germinates on the stigma, and a pollen tube grows through the style to reach the ovary. The male germ-cell travels through the pollen tube and fuses with the female gamete in the ovule — this is fertilisation. The resulting zygote divides to form an embryo. The ovule develops into a seed (with embryo and food store), and the ovary ripens into a fruit.

questions.text: Study the diagram of the longitudinal section of a flower shown in the figure. Identify the parts labelled A, B, C and D. State the function of part A and part D.

key_points: Identification of labelled parts (A=Anther, B=Stigma, C=Style, D=Ovary with ovules)
Function of A (Anther): produces pollen grains containing male germ-cells
Function of D (Ovary): contains ovules with egg cells; develops into fruit after fertilisation
rubric.expected_answer: A = Anther (produces pollen grains containing male germ-cells), B = Stigma (sticky surface that receives pollen grains), C = Style (elongated tube connecting stigma to ovary), D = Ovary (contains ovules with egg cells; develops into fruit after fertilisation).

partial_marks.2: All parts identified but functions missing

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Cross-pollination introduces greater genetic variation than self-pollination.
Reason (R): Cross-pollination involves transfer of pollen from one flower to the stigma of another flower on a different plant.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

key_points: Cross-pollination brings pollen from a different plant, combining different genetic material, thus creating more variation
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Cross-pollination brings genetic material from a different plant, leading to greater genetic variation in offspring compared to self-pollination.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of the female reproductive system in human beings?

key_points: Vas deferens is part of the male reproductive system, not female
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Vas deferens. Vas deferens is part of the male reproductive system through which sperms are delivered.

questions.text: In human beings, the fertilisation of the ovum by the sperm takes place in the:

key_points: Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube (oviduct)
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Fallopian tube (oviduct). Sperms travel upwards and reach the oviduct where they may encounter the egg. Fertilisation takes place in the fallopian tube.

questions.text: What is the role of the seminal vesicles and the prostate gland?

key_points: Seminal vesicles and prostate gland add their secretions to the sperms
The fluid makes transport of sperms easier
The fluid also provides nutrition to the sperms
rubric.expected_answer: The seminal vesicles and prostate gland add their secretions to the sperms along the path of the vas deferens. This fluid makes the transport of sperms easier and also provides nutrition to them.

questions.text: Describe the sequence of events that occur from the fertilisation of the egg to the birth of the child in humans.

key_points: Fertilised egg (zygote) starts dividing to form a ball of cells (embryo)
Embryo is implanted in the lining of the uterus
Embryo develops organs and becomes a foetus
Placenta provides nutrition and oxygen from mother's blood
Development takes approximately nine months
Child is born by rhythmic contractions of uterine muscles
rubric.expected_answer: After fertilisation in the fallopian tube, the zygote divides to form a ball of cells (embryo). The embryo is implanted in the thickened, blood-rich lining of the uterus. The placenta, a disc-like tissue embedded in the uterine wall with villi, provides a large surface area for exchange of glucose, oxygen, and waste between mother and embryo. The embryo develops organs to become a foetus over approximately nine months. Birth occurs through rhythmic contractions of the uterine muscles.

questions.text: How does the embryo get nourishment inside the mother's body? Explain the role of the placenta.

key_points: Placenta is a disc-like tissue embedded in the uterine wall
Contains villi on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side
Provides large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from mother to embryo
Also allows removal of waste from embryo to mother's blood
rubric.expected_answer: The embryo gets nourishment from the mother's blood through the placenta. The placenta is a disc-like special tissue embedded in the uterine wall. It contains villi on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side, providing a large surface area for glucose and oxygen to pass from the mother to the embryo. Waste substances from the embryo are also transferred to the mother's blood through the placenta.

questions.text: A woman has a regular menstrual cycle of 28 days. If her last menstrual period started on Day 1, on approximately which day of the cycle is ovulation most likely to occur? Show your reasoning.

key_points: Ovulation typically occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation
For a 28-day cycle: Day 28 - 14 = Day 14
rubric.expected_answer: Ovulation typically occurs approximately 14 days before the start of the next menstrual period. For a 28-day cycle: 28 - 14 = Day 14. So ovulation most likely occurs around Day 14 of the cycle.

questions.text: Describe the male reproductive system in human beings. State the function of each part. Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity?

key_points: Testes: produce sperms and secrete testosterone
Scrotum: holds testes outside body for lower temperature required for sperm formation
Vas deferens: tube that carries sperms from testes
Prostate gland and seminal vesicles: add secretions that provide nutrition and make transport easier
Urethra: common passage for sperms and urine
Penis: delivers sperms into the female reproductive tract
Testes are outside because sperm formation requires lower temperature than normal body temperature
rubric.expected_answer: The male reproductive system consists of: (1) Testes — produce sperms and secrete hormone testosterone; (2) Scrotum — sac that holds testes outside the abdominal cavity; (3) Vas deferens — tubes that carry sperms from testes; (4) Seminal vesicles and prostate gland — add secretions providing nutrition and easier transport; (5) Urethra — common passage for sperms and urine; (6) Penis — organ for delivering sperms. The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because sperm formation requires a temperature lower than normal body temperature (37°C).

partial_marks.4: Complete parts but missing scrotum explanation

questions.text: Study the diagram of the human female reproductive system shown in the figure. Identify and label the parts marked A, B, C, and D. Where does fertilisation take place?

key_points: A = Ovary (produces eggs and hormones)
B = Fallopian tube / Oviduct (carries egg from ovary to uterus)
C = Uterus (where embryo implants and develops)
D = Vagina (birth canal)
Fertilisation takes place in the fallopian tube
rubric.expected_answer: A = Ovary (produces eggs/ova and female hormones), B = Fallopian tube/Oviduct (carries egg from ovary to uterus; site of fertilisation), C = Uterus (embryo implants and develops here), D = Vagina (birth canal). Fertilisation takes place in the fallopian tube (B).

partial_marks.2: All parts identified but fertilisation site missing

questions.text: Which of the following is a mechanical barrier method of contraception?

key_points: Condom is a mechanical/physical barrier method that prevents sperm from reaching the egg
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Condom. A condom is a mechanical barrier placed on the penis (or worn in the vagina) that prevents sperms from reaching the egg.

questions.text: What are the different methods of contraception? Explain any three categories with one example each.

key_points: Barrier methods: condoms — physical barrier preventing sperm from reaching egg
Hormonal methods: oral pills — change hormonal balance so eggs are not released
IUCD methods: copper-T — placed in uterus to prevent pregnancy
Surgical methods: vasectomy (male) / tubectomy (female) — block vas deferens or fallopian tube
rubric.expected_answer: Contraceptive methods fall into several categories: (1) Barrier methods — condoms on penis or vaginal coverings create a physical barrier preventing sperm from reaching the egg; (2) Hormonal methods — oral contraceptive pills change hormonal balance so eggs are not released; (3) Intrauterine devices — copper-T placed in uterus prevents pregnancy; (4) Surgical methods — vasectomy (blocking vas deferens in males) or tubectomy (blocking fallopian tubes in females) prevents gamete transport.

questions.text: If a woman is using a copper-T, will it help in protecting her from sexually transmitted diseases? Justify your answer.

key_points: No, copper-T will not protect against STDs
Copper-T is placed in the uterus and only prevents pregnancy
It does not prevent the transmission of infections during sexual contact
Condoms provide protection against STDs
rubric.expected_answer: No, a copper-T will not help protect against sexually transmitted diseases. The copper-T is placed in the uterus and only prevents pregnancy by blocking implantation. It does not act as a barrier against the transmission of infections during sexual contact. For protection against STDs, barrier methods like condoms should be used.

questions.text: Discuss the importance of reproductive health in a society. Explain the need for adopting contraceptive methods and the significance of the legal ban on prenatal sex determination in India.

key_points: Sexual maturation does not mean the body/mind is ready for having children
STDs can be transmitted during sexual act — prevention is important
Contraception needed to avoid unwanted pregnancies affecting women's health
Population control is important for improving living standards
Prenatal sex determination banned to prevent illegal sex-selective abortion of female foetuses
Female foeticide leads to declining child sex ratio — harmful to society
rubric.expected_answer: Reproductive health is crucial for a society. The sexual act can lead to STDs (gonorrhoea, syphilis, HIV-AIDS), so awareness and prevention (condoms) are important. Unwanted pregnancies adversely affect women's health, necessitating contraceptive methods (barrier, hormonal, IUCD, surgical). Population control through contraception helps improve living standards. The legal ban on prenatal sex determination is significant because sex-selective abortion of female foetuses (female foeticide) was causing an alarming decline in the child sex ratio. A balanced female-male sex ratio is essential for a healthy society.

partial_marks.4: Complete but prenatal sex determination not covered

questions.text: The normal gestation period in humans is approximately 40 weeks. Calculate the approximate number of days of pregnancy.

key_points: Multiply weeks by 7 to get days
40 x 7 = 280 days
rubric.expected_answer: Number of days = 40 weeks x 7 days/week = 280 days. The normal gestation period in humans is approximately 280 days (about 9 months).

questions.text: The process of DNA copying during reproduction ensures:

options.text: Transfer of characters with some variations

key_points: DNA copying transfers characters from parent to offspring with minor variations
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Transfer of characters with some variations.

questions.text: What is the importance of DNA copying in reproduction? Give an example to show how variations can be useful for a species.

key_points: DNA copying is important because it transmits genetic information to next generation
It creates the blueprint for body design of offspring
Example: heat-resistant bacteria surviving global warming when others die
rubric.expected_answer: DNA copying is essential because it transfers genetic information (blueprints for body design) from parent to offspring. Minor variations during copying ensure species survival in changed environments. For example, if water temperature increases due to global warming, most bacteria would die, but heat-resistant variants would survive and reproduce, ensuring species survival.

questions.text: Which organism reproduces by multiple fission?

key_points: Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Plasmodium

questions.text: Regeneration in organisms is carried out by:

options.text: Specialised cells that can proliferate and differentiate

key_points: Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells that proliferate and form different cell types through development
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Specialised cells that can proliferate and differentiate.

questions.text: Spore formation is a mode of asexual reproduction observed in:

key_points: Rhizopus (bread mould) reproduces by spore formation using sporangia
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Rhizopus (bread mould).

questions.text: What is binary fission? Name two organisms that reproduce by binary fission.

key_points: Binary fission is a mode of asexual reproduction where the parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells
Examples: Amoeba and Leishmania (or any correct organisms)
rubric.expected_answer: Binary fission is a type of asexual reproduction in which the parent cell splits into two equal daughter cells. Two organisms that reproduce by binary fission are Amoeba and Leishmania.

questions.text: Differentiate between fragmentation and regeneration with one example each.

key_points: Fragmentation: organism breaks into fragments upon maturation, each growing into a new individual (e.g., Spirogyra)
Regeneration: if cut/broken, specialised cells regrow the complete organism from pieces (e.g., Planaria, Hydra)
rubric.expected_answer: Fragmentation: A simple multi-cellular organism breaks into smaller fragments upon maturation, and each fragment grows into a new individual. Example: Spirogyra. Regeneration: When an organism is cut or broken into pieces, specialised cells in each piece can proliferate and develop into a complete organism. Example: Planaria or Hydra.

questions.text: Why is regeneration not considered the same as reproduction? Explain.

key_points: Regeneration requires the organism to be cut/broken into pieces — it's not a normal process
Most organisms do not depend on being cut up to reproduce
Reproduction is a biological process specifically meant for producing new offspring
rubric.expected_answer: Regeneration is not the same as reproduction because most organisms do not normally depend on being cut up to be able to reproduce. Regeneration is the ability to regrow from body parts when cut, but it is not a deliberate reproductive strategy. Reproduction is a dedicated biological process for producing new offspring without requiring the parent to be damaged.

questions.text: If an Amoeba divides by binary fission once every 30 minutes, starting from a single cell, how many Amoeba cells will be present after 3 hours?

key_points: Number of fission events in 3 hours = 6 (one every 30 min)
Cells after n divisions = 2^n = 2^6 = 64
rubric.expected_answer: Number of divisions in 3 hours = 3 x 60 / 30 = 6. Number of cells = 2^6 = 64 Amoeba cells.

questions.text: Buds produced on the leaf margins of Bryophyllum can grow into new plants. This is an example of:

key_points: Bryophyllum leaf buds developing into new plants is vegetative propagation
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Vegetative propagation.

questions.text: What is vegetative propagation? Give two examples and list two advantages of this method.

key_points: Vegetative propagation is reproduction through vegetative parts (root, stem, leaves) developing into new plants
Examples: Bryophyllum (leaf buds), potato (eyes/notches), sugarcane (stem cuttings)
Advantages: faster fruiting, genetically identical to parent, can propagate seedless plants
rubric.expected_answer: Vegetative propagation is a mode of asexual reproduction in plants where parts like roots, stems, or leaves develop into new plants. Examples: (1) Bryophyllum — buds on leaf margins grow into new plants; (2) Potato — eyes on potato tubers sprout into new plants. Advantages: (1) Plants bear flowers and fruits earlier; (2) All offspring are genetically identical to the parent, preserving desirable traits.

questions.text: The female reproductive part of a flower is the:

key_points: The pistil is the female reproductive part of a flower, consisting of stigma, style and ovary
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Pistil.

questions.text: After fertilisation, the ovule in a flower develops into a:

key_points: After fertilisation, the ovule develops a tough coat and converts into a seed
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Seed. The ovule develops into a seed after fertilisation, while the ovary develops into a fruit.

questions.text: Pollen grains are produced by the:

key_points: The anther (part of stamen) produces pollen grains
rubric.expected_answer: (d) Anther.

questions.text: Name the three parts of the pistil in a flower and state the function of each.

key_points: Stigma: terminal sticky part that receives pollen grains
Style: middle elongated part connecting stigma to ovary
Ovary: swollen bottom part containing ovules with egg cells
rubric.expected_answer: The three parts of the pistil are: (1) Stigma — the terminal sticky part that receives pollen grains; (2) Style — the middle elongated tube connecting stigma to ovary; (3) Ovary — the swollen bottom part containing ovules, each with an egg cell.

questions.text: What is pollination? How does self-pollination differ from cross-pollination?

key_points: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from anther to stigma
Self-pollination: pollen transferred within the same flower
Cross-pollination: pollen transferred from one flower to another (by wind, water, animals)
rubric.expected_answer: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. In self-pollination, pollen is transferred within the same flower. In cross-pollination, pollen is transferred from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower, aided by agents like wind, water, or animals.

questions.text: Trace the path of a pollen grain from the time it lands on the stigma to the formation of a zygote in a flowering plant.

key_points: Pollen grain lands on stigma and germinates
Pollen tube grows through the style towards the ovary
Male germ-cell travels through the pollen tube
Male germ-cell fuses with female gamete (egg) in the ovule — fertilisation
The fused cell is the zygote
rubric.expected_answer: After landing on the stigma, the pollen grain germinates and a pollen tube grows out, travelling through the style to reach the ovary. The male germ-cell from the pollen grain moves through this tube. In the ovary, it reaches the ovule where the male germ-cell fuses with the female gamete (egg cell). This fusion is called fertilisation, and the resulting cell is the zygote.

questions.text: A flower has 3 carpels and each carpel contains 5 ovules. If all ovules are fertilised and each produces one seed, what is the maximum number of seeds this flower can produce?

key_points: Total seeds = number of carpels x ovules per carpel
rubric.expected_answer: Maximum number of seeds = 3 carpels x 5 ovules per carpel = 15 seeds.

questions.text: Sperms in human males are produced in the:

key_points: Sperms are produced in the testes
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Testes.

questions.text: The embryo in the uterus gets nourishment from the mother's blood through the:

key_points: The placenta provides the embryo with glucose and oxygen from mother's blood
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Placenta.

questions.text: What is menstruation? Why does it occur?

key_points: Menstruation is the breakdown and discharge of the thickened uterus lining as blood and mucous through the vagina
It occurs because the egg was not fertilised, so the thickened lining prepared for nourishing the embryo is no longer needed
Cycle takes about 28 days and lasts 2-8 days
rubric.expected_answer: Menstruation is the periodic discharge of the thickened uterus lining along with blood and mucous through the vagina. It occurs when the egg released by the ovary is not fertilised. Since no embryo needs to be nourished, the thickened, blood-rich uterus lining breaks down and is shed. This cycle occurs roughly every 28 days and lasts 2 to 8 days.

questions.text: Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotal sac in humans?

key_points: Sperm formation requires a temperature lower than normal body temperature (37°C)
The scrotum provides this lower temperature by being located outside the body cavity
rubric.expected_answer: The testes are located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotal sac because the formation of sperms requires a temperature that is lower than the normal body temperature (~37°C). The scrotum provides this cooler environment necessary for proper sperm production.

questions.text: List the changes that are seen in girls at the time of puberty.

key_points: Breast size begins to increase
Darkening of skin of nipples
Menstruation begins
Thick hair growth in armpits and genital area
Skin may become oily and pimples may develop
Growth of thinner hair on arms and legs
rubric.expected_answer: Changes in girls at puberty include: (1) Breast size begins to increase with darkening of skin of the nipples; (2) Menstruation starts; (3) Thick hair grows in armpits and genital area; (4) Skin may become oily with pimples; (5) Thinner hair may appear on arms and legs; (6) Awareness of own body increases.

questions.text: What is the role of the placenta in the development of the embryo? Explain its structure briefly.

key_points: Placenta is a disc-like tissue embedded in the uterine wall
Has villi on embryo's side and blood spaces on mother's side
Provides large surface area for exchange of nutrients and oxygen
Also removes waste from embryo to mother's blood
rubric.expected_answer: The placenta is a disc-like special tissue embedded in the uterine wall. It has villi on the embryo's side and blood spaces on the mother's side, providing a large surface area. Its role is to: (1) Allow glucose and oxygen to pass from mother's blood to the embryo for nourishment; (2) Remove waste substances from the embryo into the mother's blood for excretion.

questions.text: A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. After meiosis, how many chromosomes will be present in each sperm or egg cell?

key_points: Meiosis halves the chromosome number
rubric.expected_answer: Each sperm or egg cell will contain 46 / 2 = 23 chromosomes. Meiosis is a type of cell division that reduces the chromosome number to half, producing haploid gametes.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sexually transmitted disease?

key_points: Gonorrhoea is a bacterial sexually transmitted disease
rubric.expected_answer: (c) Gonorrhoea. It is a bacterial infection that is transmitted through sexual contact.

questions.text: Copper-T, an intrauterine device for contraception, is placed in the:

key_points: Copper-T is placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy
rubric.expected_answer: (b) Uterus. The copper-T is an intrauterine device placed in the uterus.

questions.text: Name two sexually transmitted diseases — one caused by bacteria and one caused by a virus. How can their transmission be prevented?

key_points: Bacterial STDs: gonorrhoea, syphilis
Viral STDs: warts, HIV-AIDS
Prevention: using condoms during sexual intercourse
rubric.expected_answer: Bacterial STD: Gonorrhoea (or Syphilis). Viral STD: HIV-AIDS (or Warts). Transmission can be prevented by using condoms during sexual intercourse, which act as a barrier to prevent the spread of infections.

questions.text: List three categories of contraceptive methods. Give one example of each and explain how it prevents pregnancy.

key_points: Barrier method: condom — physically prevents sperm from reaching egg
Hormonal method: oral pills — change hormonal balance so eggs are not released
Surgical method: vasectomy/tubectomy — blocks vas deferens or fallopian tube to prevent gamete transfer
rubric.expected_answer: Three categories: (1) Barrier method — condom creates a physical barrier preventing sperm from reaching the egg; (2) Hormonal method — oral contraceptive pills alter hormonal balance so eggs are not released from the ovary; (3) Surgical method — vasectomy (blocking vas deferens in males) or tubectomy (blocking fallopian tubes in females) permanently prevents gamete transport.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of natural vegetative propagation?

options.text: Formation of new plants from the eyes of a potato

key_points: Natural vegetative propagation occurs without human intervention.
Potato tubers have 'eyes' (buds) that naturally sprout into new plants under suitable conditions — this is natural vegetative propagation.
Grafting, layering, and cuttings are artificial (human-assisted) methods of vegetative propagation.
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — Formation of new plants from the eyes of a potato is natural vegetative propagation.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of vegetative propagation over seed reproduction for a fruit grower?

options.text: Vegetatively propagated plants have more genetic variation
Vegetatively propagated plants bear fruit earlier and are identical to the parent
Vegetative propagation always produces more plants than seeds

key_points: Plants from vegetative propagation are genetically identical (clones) to the parent plant.
They retain all the desirable characteristics (taste, size, yield) of the parent.
They fruit much earlier than seed-grown plants (e.g. banana, potato, sugarcane).
Seed-grown plants may show variation and take longer to mature and fruit.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Vegetatively propagated plants bear fruit earlier and are genetically identical (clones) to the parent plant, preserving all desired traits.

questions.text: In the artificial method called 'layering', a branch is bent to touch the soil and roots develop before it is cut. Which plant is commonly propagated this way?

key_points: Layering involves bending a branch to the ground, wounding it slightly, and allowing roots to develop while still attached to the parent plant.
Once roots form, the branch is cut and planted independently.
Jasmine is a classic example of layering.
Rose is propagated by cuttings; Bryophyllum by leaf margin buds; Potato by tuber eyes.
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — Jasmine is commonly propagated by layering.

questions.text: Bryophyllum (sprout-leaf plant) can grow new plants from its leaf margins. What type of vegetative propagation does this represent, and what is the name for the small plantlets formed on leaf margins?

key_points: Bryophyllum undergoes natural vegetative propagation — no human intervention needed.
Adventitious buds develop at the notches along the leaf margins.
When leaves fall to the ground, each bud can grow into a new plant.
The small plantlets formed are called 'bulbils' or, more commonly for Bryophyllum, 'epiphyllous buds' / adventitious plantlets.
rubric.expected_answer: Natural vegetative propagation via adventitious buds (epiphyllous buds/plantlets) that develop at the notches on the leaf margins. Each plantlet can grow into a complete new plant when the leaf falls.

questions.text: During DNA copying, small variations occur. Which of the following is the MOST important consequence of these variations?

options.text: They always cause disease in the offspring
They are the raw material for evolution
They prevent the offspring from surviving
They cause the offspring to look exactly like the parent

key_points: Variations introduced during DNA copying are usually minor and the offspring is mostly similar to the parent.
These variations are the raw material for evolution — over many generations, natural selection acts on variations.
Beneficial variations improve survival in changing environments; harmful ones are eliminated.
Without variation, all individuals would be identical and a single disease/environment change could wipe out an entire species.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — Variations are the raw material for evolution. Natural selection acts on these variations over generations.

questions.text: Asexual reproduction produces offspring with fewer variations than sexual reproduction. Why is this so?

options.text: Asexual reproduction does not involve any DNA
In asexual reproduction, only one parent contributes DNA, so variation comes only from DNA copying errors
Asexual reproduction uses mitosis which always produces errors
Sexual reproduction involves mutations that asexual reproduction does not

key_points: Asexual reproduction: single parent, offspring gets DNA only from that parent. Variation arises only from small errors in DNA copying (very rare).
Sexual reproduction: two parents, offspring gets DNA from both. The combination of two different DNA sets creates enormous variation through random mixing and crossing over.
Greater variation in sexual reproduction is an evolutionary advantage — populations adapt faster to environmental changes.
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — In asexual reproduction, only one parent contributes DNA, so the only source of variation is copying errors. Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents, creating much greater variation.

questions.text: A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes. After 3 such divisions, will all daughter cells have identical DNA? Explain why small variations can still occur.

key_points: In theory, binary fission produces genetically identical daughter cells — the same DNA is copied and distributed.
However, DNA copying is not perfectly error-free. Occasionally, the wrong nucleotide is inserted (mutation).
Such errors are rare but accumulate over many generations, introducing small variations.
After 3 divisions, all 8 daughter cells should be nearly identical, but rare copying errors mean tiny variations may exist.
These variations are the basis for bacterial evolution and antibiotic resistance.
rubric.expected_answer: After 3 divisions, 8 daughter cells are produced. They should be nearly identical because binary fission copies DNA faithfully. However, DNA copying is not 100% accurate — occasional errors (mutations) can introduce small variations. These rare variations are the source of evolutionary change even in asexually reproducing organisms.
